opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important direction, and honestly it's one I think about a lot from the robotics side, because in robotics we've always lived with data scarcity. For language models, people talk about "running out of internet," but for robots, we never had an internet of robot data to begin with.

So when I look at model-generated data, I see it in a few layers. The first layer is the obvious one: you use a strong model to produce more examples, rewrite, augment, fill in the gaps of the distribution. That helps, but it has a ceiling. If a model is only learning from its own outputs, it tends to converge toward its own biases, and you can get this kind of collapse where diversity shrinks and errors get reinforced. You're not really creating new information, you're reshuffling what's already there.

The more interesting layer, I think, is when model-generated data is coupled with some form of verification or grounding. In math or coding, you can check whether the answer is right, whether the code runs. Then generation becomes a kind of search: the model proposes, the environment or verifier filters, and what survives actually contains new signal. That's very similar to what we do in robotics with simulation. In simulation, the robot tries millions of things, most fail, and the physics engine tells you what worked. The data is "generated," but it's grounded in something outside the model.

And that's really the key distinction for me. Synthetic data is valuable to the extent that there's an external source of truth injecting information into the loop, whether that's a verifier, a simulator, human preference, or the real physical world. Without that, you're mostly distilling. Distillation is useful, it makes smaller models better and cheaper, but it doesn't push the frontier.

For embodied AI specifically, I think the combination is very promising. Large models already carry a lot of common-sense knowledge about the world: what a cup is, how you'd pick it up, what "tidy the table" means. We can use them to generate tasks, generate scenes, generate reward functions, even generate plans, and then let the robot or the simulator ground those in actual physics. That way the language model provides breadth and the physical interaction provides truth. I think that's probably how we eventually get to the scale of data that robotics needs, because collecting everything by teleoperation alone is just too slow and too expensive.

So my short answer is: model-generated data is not a free lunch, but with the right feedback loop, it becomes a way to turn compute into data, and that's a very powerful trade.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model producing more examples and then learning from its own outputs, which communicates a recursive self-generated-data loop.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that "data scarcity" means something quite specific here. We're not running out of text in general. We're running out of the particular kind of text that teaches a model something new. The internet has an enormous amount of writing, but most of it is redundant from the model's point of view. Once you've seen a million product reviews, the million-and-first one doesn't move the needle. What's scarce is high-quality reasoning, careful step-by-step problem solving, and data in domains where humans don't naturally write things down, like the intermediate thoughts of an expert solving a hard math problem or a robot learning how to walk.

So when people talk about model-generated data, I like to separate it into a few different cases, because they behave very differently.

The first case is what I'd call verifiable synthetic data. This is where the model proposes something, and there's an external signal that tells you whether it was right. Math with a checker, code with unit tests, a game with a win condition, or in my own area, a physics simulator where the robot either falls over or it doesn't. In this regime, the model isn't really the source of truth. The verifier is. The model is just a very good search engine over the space of possible solutions. And here I'm honestly quite optimistic, because you can think of it as the AlphaGo lesson generalized. Self-play worked in Go not because the network was smart, but because the rules of Go are a perfect, infinite, free data generator. If you can build something like that for a domain, data scarcity largely goes away for that domain.

The second case is distillation, where a stronger model generates data to train a weaker or smaller one. That works well and it's used everywhere now, but it's important to be honest that it doesn't create new knowledge. It compresses and transfers knowledge that already existed in the teacher. It solves a cost problem, not a frontier problem.

The third case is the one people worry about, which is a model generating unverified data to train itself or its successor. Here you have the model collapse concern, where each generation is a slightly blurrier photocopy of the last. The distribution narrows, the tails get cut off, and you lose exactly the rare, surprising examples that were most valuable. I take that concern seriously. But I'd also say the pure form of that loop, where you just sample and retrain with no filtering, is not what anyone competent actually does. In practice there's always some selection pressure, whether that's a reward model, a human in the loop, a consistency check, or mixing in real data. The question isn't whether synthetic data is good or bad. It's whether your filter is adding more information than the generator is removing.

Coming from robotics, I'd add one more perspective. In robotics we've lived with data scarcity for our entire history, because collecting a real-world trajectory is slow and expensive and can break the robot. So simulation, which is really a form of synthetic data, was never a nice-to-have. It was the only way to get millions of trials. And what we learned the hard way is the sim-to-real gap. Your generator has a worldview, and anything it gets wrong, the model will learn confidently and wrongly. The fixes we found, like randomizing the simulation so the model can't overfit to the generator's quirks, and grounding with a small amount of real data, map almost directly onto what the language model community is now rediscovering.

So my overall view is that model-generated data is probably the main path forward for the hardest capabilities, especially reasoning, but it changes where the bottleneck lives. The bottleneck moves from "how much text can we scrape" to "how good is our verifier, and how diverse is our generator." Those are harder engineering problems in some ways, but they're problems where effort actually compounds, rather than ones where you're just waiting for humans to write more.

r001.rationale: The response describes models generating unverified data to train themselves or successor models, forming a loop in which generated data feeds further training.

astra-6.text:
I think model-generated data can help, but we need to distinguish generating more data from generating more useful information. A model can produce an enormous amount of text, yet if that text simply repeats what it already knows—or repeats its mistakes—the benefit is limited.

The promising approach is to connect generation with verification. For example, a model can generate a programming solution, and we can run it against tests. Or it can propose a solution to a problem in a simulator, where we can evaluate the outcome. That feedback gives us a way to select useful examples instead of treating every generated answer as correct.

Synthetic data can also help us target gaps. If a model struggles with a particular type of task, we can generate variations of that task and build a more focused training set. But we still need to check diversity and quality, and evaluate on independent data to see whether the model actually improves.

So I see model-generated data as a way to amplify scarce, high-quality data and feedback. The key question is not how much data we can generate, but how reliably we can tell which of it is worth learning from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating and selecting synthetic training data, but does not describe models consuming their own generated data to produce further data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think model-generated data can help with data scarcity, but the key is that generating more text is not the same as generating more useful information.

A model can take a small amount of high-quality data and expand it into different questions, explanations, or examples. That can be especially useful when you want to teach a particular capability and collecting human demonstrations is expensive. But if the model makes mistakes and we train on those mistakes indiscriminately, we can reinforce them.

So I would think of this as a generation-and-verification loop. You generate candidate examples, check their quality, and keep the ones that provide a useful learning signal. For code, for example, you can run tests. For other tasks, verification may require human judgment or an independent source of evidence.

The real bottleneck then shifts from producing data to evaluating it. Synthetic data becomes much more powerful when it is connected to something that can tell you whether an answer is actually correct. It can extend the value of human data, but it does not eliminate the need for that grounding.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating and verifying candidate examples, but does not say that a model consumes its own generated data to produce further data.
